msg: During the second preaching tour, after teaching about anger, Jesus went on in the same setting to speak of the importance of “⟦Q 149:4.3⟧possessing well-balanced characters.⟦/Q⟧” He recognized that it was necessary for most men to devote themselves to the mastery of some vocation. But he deplored the tendency toward overspecialization, toward becoming “⟦Q 149:4.3⟧narrow-minded and circumscribed in life’s activities.⟦/Q⟧” When we are absorbed in only one thing, other parts of the personality easily wither. Jesus wanted people to grow as whole persons, not only in a single talent. His concern was always for the growth of the whole person, not merely a part.

What stands out especially in Jesus’ teaching is his observation that “⟦Q 149:4.3⟧any virtue, if carried to extremes, may become a vice.⟦/Q⟧” Sympathy and pity are beautiful virtues, but “⟦Q 149:4.3⟧overmuch sympathy and pity may degenerate into serious emotional instability.⟦/Q⟧” Enthusiasm is a precious force, but when it loses its balance, it “⟦Q 149:4.3⟧may drive on into fanaticism.⟦/Q⟧” Imagination is a source of creativity, but cut off from reality it drifts into fantasy. On the other hand, “⟦Q 149:4.3⟧the dullness of overconservative mediocrity⟦/Q⟧” is dangerous too. Jesus “⟦Q 149:4.3⟧always preached temperance and taught consistency — proportionate adjustment of life problems.⟦/Q⟧”

This teaching is best seen in Jesus’ own life. The Urantia Book portrays his personality as wonderfully balanced. He was courageous but not reckless, gentle but not weak, enthusiastic but never fanatical (see Paper 100). He mingled deeply with people yet never lost his times of solitary communion with the Father; he was earnest yet never lost his joy and humor. It was this harmony that made his personality so attractive.

In the life of faith, too, balance is vitally important. To be so absorbed in spiritual things that we neglect everyday responsibilities, and to be so buried in everyday life that we lose the spiritual life, are both forms of lopsidedness. Character grows healthy when prayer and work, personal devotion and service to our neighbors, conviction about truth and tolerance for other views hold one another up. Religious zeal in particular can easily run to extremes, so the greater our enthusiasm, the more wisdom and humility must grow alongside it. The stronger our convictions, the more we need the humility to remain open to the possibility that we may be wrong; and the more zealous we are in helping others, the more we need the wisdom to care for ourselves.

Balance is not the same as lukewarmness. The temperance Jesus spoke of is not a listless middle way of doing everything moderately, but the maturity that brings each virtue into harmony with the others. A virtue becomes whole when love is joined by wisdom, courage by discernment, and conviction by humility. Such harmony is not produced by willpower alone; it comes about gradually as we entrust ourselves to the guidance of the indwelling spirit. A life led by the spirit does not lean to one side; it is a life in which every part finds its place and blends with the rest.

Today, look back over your life and see whether any part leans too far to one side. If you are too bound up in work, tend to rest and relationships; if you are all thought, begin some small practice; if you are worn out from helping others, take time to rest in the Father. A balanced character is not achieved overnight, but small daily adjustments add up until we grow into a whole personality that resembles Jesus.
d294.pr: Find one area of your life that leans too far to one side, and set aside a little time today for its opposite.

msg: During the second preaching tour, the apostles asked Jesus about the phrase “⟦Q 149:6.5⟧the fear of the Lord.⟦/Q⟧” The Hebrew scriptures say that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, yet Jesus taught that God is a loving Father. In answering, Jesus explained how man’s attitude toward God has grown, and today’s passage is the heart of that teaching. It is a question that many believers still carry in their hearts today.

Jesus first understands the fear of the forebears: “⟦Q 149:6.5⟧Your forebears feared God because he was mighty and mysterious.⟦/Q⟧” It is natural that “⟦Q 149:6.5⟧the power of God engenders fear in the heart of man.⟦/Q⟧” The Urantia Book explains that the religion of primitive mankind began in fear of the unknown forces of nature (see Paper 86). But as revelation advanced, people came to know God’s personality more deeply than his power, and “⟦Q 149:6.5⟧the nobility and righteousness of his personality beget reverence, love, and willing worship.⟦/Q⟧”

Jesus sums up the purpose of his coming into the world in four contrasts: “⟦Q 149:6.5⟧to put love in the place of fear, joy in the place of sorrow, confidence in the place of dread, loving service and appreciative worship in the place of slavish bondage and meaningless ceremonies.⟦/Q⟧” This sentence holds the very essence of Jesus’ gospel. The relationship between God and man is not that of master and slave but of Father and child, and the power that moves that relationship is not fear but love. To people who had thought of God only as a fearsome judge, he showed the face of a Father who waits for his children and welcomes them home.

Jesus gives the example of a dutiful and affectionate son: “⟦Q 149:6.5⟧A dutiful and affectionate son does not fear or dread even a mighty and noble father.⟦/Q⟧” He knows his father’s strength, but he knows that this strength exists within a love directed toward him. So it is with the children of God. We are humbled before God’s infinite power, yet we trust that this power seeks not to harm us but to protect and guide us. And so reverence remains while dread vanishes. Fear makes people shrink, but reverence born of love makes them free and bold.

Even so, Jesus acknowledges that for “⟦Q 149:6.5⟧those who sit in darkness,⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 149:6.5⟧the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.⟦/Q⟧” There are stages in the growth of faith. But “⟦Q 149:6.5⟧when the light has more fully come, the sons of God are led to praise the Infinite for what he is rather than to fear him for what he does.⟦/Q⟧” Mature worship is not an attempt to gain or avoid something; it is a response to the beauty and goodness of God himself. This is true worship, which asks for nothing and is offered only in gratitude and love.

Where does our faith stand today? If we pray out of fear of punishment, or for fear of missing a blessing, we are still dwelling in a religion of fear. Meditate quietly on who God is. When we think of the One who is “⟦Q 149:6.5⟧magnificent in love, plenteous in mercy, and glorious in truth,⟦/Q⟧” our worship becomes a joy rather than a duty, and fear is gradually transformed into trust. And the more we come to know the Father in this way, the more our prayers will be filled with shorter requests and longer thanksgiving.
d295.pr: Today, ask God for nothing, and offer him only thanks and praise for who he is.

msg: At the start of the third preaching tour, Jesus sent his apostles out two by two to the cities of Galilee. Before they set out, he did not hide from them the difficulties ahead. People might reject them, and persecution might follow. Yet Jesus did not send them out in fear. Pointing to the commonplace sight of two sparrows sold for a penny, he reminded them how minute God’s care is. The apostles must have felt the weight of going out for the first time to preach the gospel on their own, without their Master.

Even the cheapest bird in the market is not forgotten in God’s sight. “⟦Q 150:4.3⟧The very hairs of your head are all numbered.⟦/Q⟧” This means that God does not govern the universe loosely but knows and cares for even the smallest things. The Urantia Book teaches that the Universal Father knows all things and that his love is directed to each individual (see Paper 3). So Jesus’ conclusion is clear: “⟦Q 150:4.3⟧Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than a great many sparrows.⟦/Q⟧” These words are a comfort not only to the apostles but to everyone who lives in anxiety today.

On the ground of this assurance, Jesus asks his apostles for boldness: “⟦Q 150:4.3⟧Be not ashamed of my teaching; go forth proclaiming peace and good will.⟦/Q⟧” But he also warns against naive optimism: “⟦Q 150:4.3⟧peace will not always attend your preaching.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus came to bring peace on earth, but “⟦Q 150:4.3⟧when men reject my gift, division and turmoil result.⟦/Q⟧” Truth brings peace to those who receive it, but it can also create tension with those who reject it. So when we are rejected, we should neither lose heart nor grow angry, but keep a peaceful spirit and take the next step.

Jesus speaks in particular of division within the family. When the whole family receives the gospel, true peace abides in that house, but when only some receive it, sorrow may follow. Jesus urges them to “⟦Q 150:4.3⟧labor earnestly to save the whole family.⟦/Q⟧” He does not tell them to abandon their families, but to love them with all their hearts and lead them toward truth. Only if, after they have done their utmost, the moment of choice still comes, they must put God’s will before all else. To those torn between love for family and loyalty to truth, Jesus teaches that neither should be lightly cast aside.

Jesus himself walked this path. For a long time his family did not understand his mission, and at one point they even tried to take him home (see Paper 154). Yet Jesus did not resent his family; he loved them to the end. He knew that doing the Father’s will and loving his family would in the end come together as one. And indeed his brother James later took part in the early Christian movement (154:6.9).

We too live amid many fears today. The opinions of others, conflicts in our relationships, and an unknown future make us shrink back. At such times, remember the sparrows. If God does not forget even one small bird, how could he forget a child who bears his spirit? With this assurance we can live boldly as people who are not ashamed of the truth and who carry peace and good will to others.
d296.pr: Write down one fear that makes you shrink back today, and beside it write, “I am of more value than sparrows.”

msg: During the third preaching tour, the question the apostles heard most often was this: What must I do to be saved? Jesus taught them in detail how to answer it, and today’s passage is the final statement in which he summed up that teaching. It is a short paragraph, but it holds the very heart of Jesus’ gospel. This question rises from the depths of every human soul, across every age and culture.

The first principle is that “⟦Q 150:5.5⟧you cannot buy salvation; you cannot earn righteousness.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 150:5.5⟧Salvation is the gift of God, and righteousness is the natural fruit of the spirit-born life of sonship.⟦/Q⟧” Many religions have taught that people must win God’s favor by accumulating good works, rituals, and sacrifices. But Jesus reverses the order: “⟦Q 150:5.5⟧You are not to be saved because you live a righteous life; rather is it that you live a righteous life because you have already been saved, have recognized sonship as the gift of God.⟦/Q⟧” A gift is not bought at a price but received with gratitude. All we need do is receive that gift by faith.

In the preceding paragraph Jesus summed up the way of salvation like this: believe the gospel, accept divine forgiveness, and recognize by faith the spirit of God who dwells within (150:5.2). By this faith we are justified, saved, and carried forward forever on the path of divine perfection (150:5.3). Entrance into the Father’s kingdom is wholly free, but continuing within it requires progress, growth in grace. The entrance stands wide open by grace, but the life within is a life of daily growth.

The second principle is that “⟦Q 150:5.5⟧realization of sonship is incompatible with the desire to sin.⟦/Q⟧” This is a profound insight. People worry that emphasizing grace will lead to moral license. But Jesus says the opposite is true. Those who truly believe in the goodness of God “⟦Q 150:5.5⟧will be led to voluntary repentance of all known sin.⟦/Q⟧” The deeper our awareness that we are beloved children, the more foreign and distasteful it becomes to act against that love. Grace does not make us take sin lightly; it is the power that makes us no longer want to sin.

That is why Jesus says that “⟦Q 150:5.5⟧kingdom believers hunger for righteousness and thirst for divine perfection.⟦/Q⟧” Their good works do not spring from the compulsion of law or the fear of punishment, but from the longing of God’s children to become like their Father. And they regard “⟦Q 150:5.5⟧service in the kingdom as the supreme delight of life on earth.⟦/Q⟧” Duty transformed into delight: this is the mark of the reborn life. So their service carries no strain but a natural joy.

Today we may lay down the labor of trying to prove ourselves before God. Accept by faith the fact that you have already been received as the Father’s child. Then do the good that springs from that joy. A life striving to earn salvation and a life lived in the gratitude of the saved may look alike on the outside, but within they are entirely different. The first breeds anxiety; the second brings peace and freedom. To begin the day with gratitude is the most natural first step of a child who has been saved.
d297.pr: Do one good thing today not “in order to be saved” but “because I am the Father’s child.”

d298.t: Leaving the Results to the Father
msg: After Jesus had told the parable of the sower by the seaside, the apostles debated its meaning all evening. Peter tried to attach symbolic meaning to every detail of the parable, and the others offered their own interpretations. As the discussion grew long and confused, Thomas rose and reminded them of a principle Jesus had taught earlier: a parable is meant to teach one great truth, not to have every detail interpreted allegorically. At Andrew’s request, Thomas then shared the one truth he had understood.

The truth Thomas saw was this: “⟦Q 151:2.6⟧our teaching of the gospel of the kingdom, no matter how faithfully and efficiently we execute our divine commissions, is going to be attended by varying degrees of success; and that all such differences in results are directly due to conditions inherent in the circumstances of our ministry, conditions over which we have little or no control.⟦/Q⟧” The sower scattered the same seed with the same hand, yet the wayside, the rocky ground, the thorns, and the good soil each yielded a different harvest. The fault lay neither with the seed nor with the sower. It was the condition of the soil that made the difference.

This interpretation was a deep comfort to the apostles. Not long before, they had seen their Master rejected at Nazareth (150:9), and they were disappointed to see so many seeking miracles rather than the gospel. Thomas’s words reminded them that results falling short of their hopes did not necessarily mean their own failure or the powerlessness of the gospel. “⟦Q 151:2.6⟧The words which Thomas spoke had a quieting effect on all of them,⟦/Q⟧” and the discussion became a precious lesson in how to understand parables.

This truth applies just as fully to all our service today. Parents teaching their children, teachers teaching their students, believers sharing truth with their neighbors are all sowers. We are responsible for sowing the seed as best we can, but when and how that seed will sprout is not in our hands. The human heart moves according to its own free choices and countless conditions we cannot know. Once we begin to judge ourselves by results, we easily become proud or easily lose heart. Our worth is measured not by the size of the harvest but by our faithfulness to our commission.

Yet this teaching does not mean we may be careless. Thomas clearly added the condition: “⟦Q 151:2.6⟧no matter how faithfully and efficiently we execute our divine commissions.⟦/Q⟧” We must choose our seed with care, watch for the right season, and strive to understand the soil. That is why Jesus taught them to present truth in keeping with people’s intellectual level and disposition (151:3.1). But once we have done our best, we must lay down our anxiety about the results and leave them to the Father. For it is God who gives the growth.

If, among the things you labor at today, there is one that has worn you out because no fruit appears, remember this parable. The seed we sow is not wasted. Some seeds sprout only after a long time, and some bear fruit in places we will never see. Faithfulness is our part; the harvest is the Father’s. When we accept this distinction, we can become sowers who sow joyfully, without discouragement and without pride.
d298.pr: Call to mind one task that has worn you out because no fruit appears, pray that you leave the results to the Father, and faithfully do just your part today.

d299.t: The Seed That Grows by Itself
msg: On that evening when the apostles were wholly absorbed in parables, Jesus, before dismissing the group, told them the last of the parable of the sower. A man cast good seed upon the earth, and while he slept by night and went about his business by day, the seed sprang up and grew and came to fruit. He did not know how it came about. “⟦Q 151:3.15⟧First there was the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.⟦/Q⟧” And when the grain was ripe, he put forth the sickle and the harvest was finished.

This short parable holds a profound insight into the way the kingdom of heaven grows. The kingdom is not forced into growth by human effort; it grows by the power of life within the seed. The sower’s task is to sow and to wait, and the mysterious process of growth takes place beyond his understanding and control. Jesus said he wished to test how they would receive this, perhaps to awaken them from their impatience for quick results. Life belongs to God, and man is only a co-worker who prepares the conditions in which that life can grow.

This parable fits perfectly the spiritual growth that takes place within the individual soul. The Urantia Book teaches that much of spiritual growth takes place below the level of consciousness, through the quiet activity of the indwelling Thought Adjuster. We do not feel our souls growing from day to day. Yet as we go on accepting truth and choosing the Father’s will, an unseen growth continues within us. Then one day, looking back, we discover that a patience and love once impossible for us have grown up within.

The parable also shows that growth has its order and its stages. First the blade, then the ear, and last the full grain. It would be foolish to look at the blade and demand to know why it is not yet grain. Yet we easily harbor just this impatience, toward ourselves and toward others. We demand mature fruit from someone who has only just begun to believe, or we condemn ourselves because we are still lacking. But God treasures each stage, and the blade is as much an expression of life as the grain.

Another lesson of this parable is rest. The sower slept at night. He did not fret, watching over the seed all night long. He did his part and left the rest to the order of the soil and of life. Our spiritual lives need this restful trust as well. Anxiously checking our spiritual condition all the time actually hinders growth. Once we have accepted truth and trusted the Father, we must set our minds at ease and let his spirit work within us.

Today, think of the seeds that have been sown within you and within those you love. Even if nothing seems to be changing now, life is growing where it cannot be seen. We need only be faithful in sowing and watering, and wait in trust upon the One who gives the growth. In due time the ear will appear and the grain will ripen. As Jesus said, “⟦Q 151:3.15⟧He who has an ear to hear, let him hear.⟦/Q⟧” May this be a day of listening to the wisdom of this quiet trust.
d299.pr: Find one area of spiritual growth in you that is still only a blade, and resolve to watch over it with gratitude rather than impatience.

msg: After feeding the five thousand, Jesus prayed alone in the hills, then returned to Bethsaida and sat down with his apostles. Having eaten the miraculous bread, the multitude had tried to make him king, and some of the apostles had been swept up in that fervor (152:3). Lamenting how much longer he must bear with them, Jesus rebuked them for being ruled by material motives. Today’s passage is the question and teaching Jesus put to them following that rebuke.

The first thing Jesus points to is the limitation of miracles: “⟦Q 152:5.4⟧the working of miracles and the performance of material wonders will not win souls for the spiritual kingdom.⟦/Q⟧” The multitude was fed, “⟦Q 152:5.4⟧but it did not lead them to hunger for the bread of life neither to thirst for the waters of spiritual righteousness.⟦/Q⟧” Instead, once their hunger was satisfied, they sought not entrance into the kingdom of heaven but to proclaim the Son of Man king, “⟦Q 152:5.4⟧only that they might continue to eat bread without having to toil therefor.⟦/Q⟧” Material satisfaction more often lulls spiritual longing to sleep than awakens it. Those whose stomachs are full do not look up to heaven.

This event was a watershed in Jesus’ public ministry. The Urantia Book says that the feeding of the five thousand and the attempt to make him king marked the height of popular acclaim for Jesus, and at the same time the peak of the people’s miracle-seeking (152:6.5). Soon the Capernaum crisis came, and after Jesus’ sermon on the bread of life, many of his followers fell away (see Paper 153). Even at the cost of his popularity, Jesus would not allow his mission to be turned into the role of a material Messiah.

Jesus also says that all this “⟦Q 152:5.4⟧does nothing to reveal the heavenly Father or to advance his kingdom on earth.⟦/Q⟧” The apostles thought that making him king would hasten the kingdom, but in fact it was a foolish course that would turn even the civil rulers into enemies. Every attempt to accomplish spiritual ends by political or material means always damages the end itself. The kingdom of God is not built by power or the enthusiasm of crowds; it is built when the Father’s will takes root in the heart of each individual.

These words put a sharp question to the communities of faith of our own day. With what are we trying to draw people? It is easy to gather people with programs and benefits, comfort and entertainment, but whether those who gather in this way truly come to hunger for the bread of life is another matter. Feeding the hungry is, of course, a precious service. But when service drifts away from its aim of leading people to the Father and becomes an end in itself, we may repeat the mistake of giving bread and losing souls.

Jesus ends this rebuke with a prayer: “⟦Q 152:5.4⟧I pray that the Father will anoint your eyes that you may see and open your ears that you may hear.⟦/Q⟧” Even in his disappointment he did not give up on his apostles. Today we too can offer this prayer for ourselves. Ask that eyes clouded by material motives may be opened to see spiritual reality, and that we may become people who long for the bread of life more than for bread. When that prayer is answered, we will see a miracle greater than any miracle: a transformed soul.
d300.pr: Honestly identify one thing you expect from your faith that springs from a material motive.

msg: On the day of his sermon on the bread of life in the synagogue at Capernaum, Jesus’ public ministry reached a great turning point. Many who had followed him in hope of miracles and bread stumbled over his spiritual teaching and left his side one by one. That Saturday evening, before his discouraged and perplexed apostles, Jesus spoke the words of today’s passage. They were at once his comfort to them and a solemn question to their faith. Seeing those who only yesterday had wanted to make him king now turning their backs, the apostles must have been very heavy of heart.

Jesus first reminds them that “⟦Q 153:5.4⟧it is the spirit that quickens; the flesh and all that pertains thereto is of little profit.⟦/Q⟧” The people had left because they sought the bread of the flesh. They hoped the Messiah would come and make their earthly lives comfortable, but Jesus had come to proclaim spiritual liberty, teach eternal truth, and foster living faith (153:2.6). “⟦Q 153:5.4⟧The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life,⟦/Q⟧” and to those who did not seek spiritual things those words became a stumbling block.

Jesus says that “⟦Q 153:5.4⟧from the beginning I knew that these halfhearted believers would fall out by the way.⟦/Q⟧” The enthusiasm of the crowd was not rooted in spiritual conviction, so it could not last. Trials sift faith. In easy times it is hard to tell who are true disciples, but when the time comes to pay a price, it becomes clear where each person’s faith is rooted. That is why Jesus urges his apostles: “⟦Q 153:5.4⟧Let each of you look to his own faith.⟦/Q⟧” A time of trial is not a time meant to destroy us, but a time that honestly reveals what our faith rests upon.

Then Jesus asks a question that stirs the heart: “⟦Q 153:5.4⟧And now at such a time as this would you also desert?⟦/Q⟧” Peter answered that though they were sad and perplexed, they would never forsake him; he had taught them the words of eternal life, and they knew he was sent by God. This confession did not come from understanding everything. It came from trusting, even in perplexity, the person of Jesus and the life contained in his words.

Such moments come to our faith as well. When the answer we hoped for does not come, when our faith costs us something, when those around us leave one by one, the question rises within us too: Should I also leave? What we can hold on to then is not an answer that explains everything, but trust like Peter’s confession: I do not understand it all, but I know there is life in this truth. That simple conviction carries us through the night of perplexity.

Jesus also says, “⟦Q 153:5.4⟧Be of good cheer! I have not deserted you.⟦/Q⟧” Even when we waver, he does not leave us. Today, quietly examine your faith. Why am I walking this path? Is it for bread, or for the words of life? Only those who stand honestly before that question can become faithful disciples who remain at the Master’s side even in hard days. The decision to stay with him, as Peter did, even in perplexity, will make our faith deeper still.
d301.pr: Write in one sentence why you keep walking the path of faith, and see whether it is for bread or for the words of life.

msg: After the Capernaum crisis had passed, Jesus and his apostles spent a week of rest even under the pressure of hostile forces. In recording this period, The Urantia Book sets forth an important principle: “⟦Q 154:2.5⟧Universe difficulties must be met and planetary obstacles must be encountered as a part of the experience training provided for the growth and development, the progressive perfection, of the evolving souls of mortal creatures.⟦/Q⟧” When we consider the situation of Jesus and his apostles as they passed through this season of trial, the principle carries all the more weight.

The heart of this paragraph is that spiritual growth does not come from ease. “⟦Q 154:2.5⟧The spiritualization of the human soul requires intimate experience with the educational solving of a wide range of real universe problems.⟦/Q⟧” The soul does not grow by avoiding problems. Mind, soul, and spirit grow together in the process of wrestling with problems, choosing, failing, and rising again. The passage states flatly that “⟦Q 154:2.5⟧the animal nature and the lower forms of will creatures do not progress favorably in environmental ease.⟦/Q⟧” Just as a hothouse plant cannot withstand the wind, a soul that has never known trials is easily shaken.

This connects with a teaching The Urantia Book stresses in many places. Here lies the reason the Universal Father permits uncertainty, difficulty, and danger on the evolutionary worlds. For courage grows in the face of danger, patience amid delay, faith amid uncertainty, and love before those who are hard to love (see Paper 3). In a world with no difficulties at all, there would be no soil in which these virtues could grow. God does not permit difficulties in order to make us suffer; he uses them as material for growth in order to make us mature.

The passage says that the stimulus to growth arises when “⟦Q 154:2.5⟧problematic situations, coupled with exertion stimuli,⟦/Q⟧” work together. Difficulty alone is not enough. If we give up or run away in the face of difficulty, it leaves not growth but a wound. But when difficulty is joined with effort, it awakens “⟦Q 154:2.5⟧those activities of mind, soul, and spirit⟦/Q⟧” which carry us on toward “⟦Q 154:2.5⟧higher levels of spirit destiny.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus himself did not avoid the countless difficulties of his earth life but met them head-on, and in doing so he passed personally through the whole range of human experience.

When we accept this principle in daily life, our attitude toward difficulties changes. Problems at work, conflicts in relationships, limitations of health, and financial hardship all feel like unwelcome guests. Yet at the same time they are classrooms in which our souls can grow. When difficulty comes, if instead of asking “Why me?” we ask “What can I learn from this, and how can I grow?”, the same situation takes on an entirely different meaning.

Of course, this is not a call to seek out pain deliberately, nor to brush off other people’s difficulties lightly as opportunities for growth. It is simply an invitation not to lose heart before unavoidable problems, but to work them out together with the Father’s spirit. Look today with new eyes at the difficulty set before you. The very place where you wrestle with it can become the place where your soul grows a hand’s breadth closer to heaven. The Father does not leave us alone in that place of wrestling; he is there with us through the indwelling spirit.
d302.pr: Write down one difficulty you are facing, and beside it write one virtue that could grow in you through it.

msg: While fleeing through northern Galilee, on the way to Phoenicia, Jesus preached on true religion to the apostles and evangelists who were with him. He distinguished two kinds of religion. One is the religion of authority, a religion of the mind based on tradition and theology; the other is the religion of the spirit, based on personal experience of God. Today’s passage sharply describes what those who prefer to remain in the religion of authority lose.

The passage says that “⟦Q 155:5.10⟧for a long time there will live on earth those timid, fearful, and hesitant individuals who will prefer thus to secure their religious consolations.⟦/Q⟧” They cast their lot with the religions of authority. They want others or institutions to decide for them what to believe and how to live. That seems comfortable and safe. But the price is that “⟦Q 155:5.10⟧they compromise the sovereignty of personality, debase the dignity of self-respect,⟦/Q⟧” and surrender the right to share in the most inspiring experience a human being can know. Yet a path walked for us by someone else can never become our own.

What is that experience? The passage describes it in many layers: “⟦Q 155:5.10⟧the personal quest for truth, the exhilaration of facing the perils of intellectual discovery, the determination to explore the realities of personal religious experience,⟦/Q⟧” and the victory of spiritual faith over intellectual doubt. All of these finally come together as one: “⟦Q 155:5.10⟧the supreme adventure of all human existence — man seeking God, for himself and as himself, and finding him.⟦/Q⟧” No one can undertake this adventure for us.

Jesus was not telling them to disregard authority or tradition as such. He loved the Hebrew scriptures and quoted them often. But he warned against substituting another person’s experience for one’s own. In the paragraph that follows, Jesus says that the religion of the spirit means effort, struggle, conflict, faith, determination, love, loyalty, and progress (155:5.11). The religion of the spirit is not easy, for we must go out and find truth for ourselves amid uncertainty, with no sure answers handed to us in advance.

But on that path there is a joy the religion of authority can never give. Not a God I have heard about from others but a God I have met, not a truth known by memorizing it but a truth known by living it, gives our souls an indelible assurance. Even when doubts come, a faith won by honestly wrestling with them becomes deeper and firmer than before. That is why the passage calls this experience “⟦Q 155:5.10⟧the supreme satisfaction.⟦/Q⟧” Nothing enriches the soul like the triumph of a faith honestly won. Such a faith does not collapse at a single word from someone else; it stands like a deep-rooted tree in the winds of trial.

Look at your faith today. Am I seeking God for myself, or resting content with answers someone else has set for me? Do not be afraid to ask questions. Honest doubt is not the enemy of faith; it can become a door into deeper faith. The indwelling spirit of the Father is waiting for us to set out in search of truth for ourselves. Take one step of that adventure today.
d303.pr: Write down one question about faith you have been afraid to ask, and resolve to seek its answer honestly.

d304.t: The Soul That Feels the Presence
msg: On the road to Phoenicia, Jesus went on with his second discourse on religion. If the first discourse distinguished between the religion of authority and the religion of the spirit, this one taught how those born of the spirit actually hear the word of God and experience his presence. Today’s passage is an especially practical portion of it. Jesus says, “⟦Q 155:6.12⟧You must cease to seek for the word of God only on the pages of the olden records of theologic authority.⟦/Q⟧” To people of that time, who revered the letter of scripture, this must have been a startling statement.

Jesus was not telling them to disregard the scriptures. He knew the scriptures more deeply than anyone and quoted them often. What he warned against was the idea that the word of God is locked within the records of a single age. Just before this, he had said that the Father did not cease to speak words of truth to the world after speaking through the prophets of old (155:6.2). “⟦Q 155:6.12⟧Those who are born of the spirit of God shall henceforth discern the word of God regardless of whence it appears to take origin. Divine truth must not be discounted because the channel of its bestowal is apparently human.⟦/Q⟧”

At the center of the passage lies the distinction between theory and experience. “⟦Q 155:6.12⟧Many of your brethren have minds which accept the theory of God while they spiritually fail to realize the presence of God.⟦/Q⟧” Knowing about God and knowing God are different. Assenting to theological propositions is the work of the head, but feeling the presence of God is the work of the soul. That is why Jesus says, “⟦Q 155:6.12⟧It is not so important that you should know about the fact of God as that you should increasingly grow in the ability to feel the presence of God.⟦/Q⟧” Knowledge can point to the door that leads to God, but it is the experience of faith that opens it and goes in.

As the way to cultivate that ability, Jesus offers the spiritual attitude of a sincere child. But he makes a clear distinction: “⟦Q 155:6.12⟧It is not the mental immaturity of the child that I commend to you but rather the spiritual simplicity of such an easy-believing and fully-trusting little one.⟦/Q⟧” Our thinking should be mature and our discernment keen, but before God our hearts should be as simple and open as a child held in its father’s arms. Intellectual maturity and spiritual simplicity do not conflict; rather, they complete each other.

In the paragraph that follows, Jesus says that once we begin to find God in our own souls, we will soon find him in the souls of others, and at last in all the creatures of the universe (155:6.13). But he laments that men give so little time to contemplating such eternal realities. The ability to feel God’s presence does not grow by itself. Only with times of quiet stillness, times of worship and communion, does that sense awaken and grow. Deliberately making such times amid a busy life is the starting point of spiritual growth.

Today, does your faith stop at knowledge about God, or is it growing toward feeling God’s presence? For even a moment during the day, lay aside all your thoughts and rest like a child before the Father’s spirit within you. And listen to discern the word of God in what you read today, in the people you meet, and in the nature around you. When you do, God will draw near not as a concept in a book but as a living presence.
d304.pr: For five minutes today, ask for nothing and rest quietly, like a child, in the Father’s presence.

msg: During their stay at Tyre and Sidon, Jesus and the apostles taught among the gentiles. The Jews regarded gentiles as people outside God’s covenant, yet the gentile believers of Sidon “⟦Q 156:2.4⟧in many ways⟦/Q⟧” appreciated Jesus’ teachings “⟦Q 156:2.4⟧more fully than the Jews.⟦/Q⟧” For the apostles this was a startling experience, for those they had considered far from God grasped the heart of the gospel better than they did. This experience became an important occasion for breaking down the apostles’ long-held prejudices. They saw with their own eyes that God’s truth is received not through lineage or tradition but through an open heart.

What did these gentiles understand? First, they “⟦Q 156:2.4⟧came to know not only that Jesus was like God but also that God was like Jesus.⟦/Q⟧” This is a very deep insight. The confession that Jesus is divine is important, but even more revolutionary is the realization that God is as loving, merciful, and approachable as Jesus. Through the life of Jesus we see the character of God. This is why The Urantia Book again and again presents Jesus as the one who reveals the Father.

Second, they understood the teaching about “⟦Q 156:2.4⟧the uniformity of the laws of this world and the entire universe.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 156:2.4⟧God is no respecter of persons, races, or nations; … there is no favoritism with the Universal Father; … the universe is wholly and ever law-abiding and unfailingly dependable.⟦/Q⟧” This teaching was hard to accept for Jews steeped in the idea of a chosen people, but for the gentiles it was news of liberation. Before God no one is privileged, and no one is excluded. This truth also puts a searching question to the way we regard people of other religions and cultures today.

The passage says, “⟦Q 156:2.4⟧These gentiles were not afraid of Jesus; they dared to accept his message.⟦/Q⟧” And at the end it adds a profound insight: “⟦Q 156:2.4⟧All down through the ages men have not been unable to comprehend Jesus; they have been afraid to.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus’ teachings are not difficult at all. The truth that God is our Father and all people are brothers is something even a child can understand. The problem is that accepting that truth means our lives must change.

Why are we afraid to understand Jesus? If we take his teachings seriously, we must love our enemies, give up our prejudices, and lay down the thought that we are superior. We may have to leave familiar traditions and safe enclosures. So we try to wrap his simple words in complicated doctrines or postpone them as distant ideals. Pretending not to understand is easier than understanding and following. Often what we lack for knowing the truth is not intellect but the courage to follow it.

Can we today, like the gentiles of Sidon, receive Jesus’ message without fear? Honestly face one of his teachings that you know but have been avoiding. If we believe that God is like Jesus, we have no reason to be afraid before him. And if we believe in a Father who loves all people without favoritism, we too can cross the walls of prejudice and welcome everyone as a brother or sister.
d305.pr: Find one teaching of Jesus you have known but put off practicing, and carry it out today, however modestly.

msg: At Tyre Jesus gave his apostles and evangelists a profound teaching on temptation and self-mastery. He first acknowledged the conflict within human nature between lower desires and higher ideals. Then, in today’s passage, he clearly distinguishes the wrong way and the right way of dealing with that conflict. This is a very practical teaching for anyone who has wrestled with temptation, and its wisdom holds just as true for believers today.

The wrong way Jesus warns against is “⟦Q 156:5.5⟧undertaking to surmount temptation by the effort of supplanting one desire by another and supposedly superior desire through the mere force of the human will.⟦/Q⟧” Gritting our teeth and enduring, or forcibly holding down a bad habit, cannot truly overcome temptation. Such a method may seem to work for a while, but in the end it leaves us “⟦Q 156:5.5⟧increasingly overburdened with the deceptive suppression of mortal desires.⟦/Q⟧” Suppressed desires do not disappear; they wait for their chance, and we grow weary of the endless inner battle. A struggle sustained by willpower alone collapses at the moment the will grows weak.

The right way Jesus presents is spiritual transformation: to have “⟦Q 156:5.5⟧really and truly developed an actual interest in, and love for, those higher and more idealistic forms of conduct⟦/Q⟧” that we wish to substitute for the lower habits of behavior we recognize as temptation. In other words, rather than spending our strength hating what is bad, we should set our hearts on loving what is good. Then “⟦Q 156:5.5⟧the old and the inferior will be forgotten in the love for the new and the superior.⟦/Q⟧” It is like switching on a light instead of struggling to drive the darkness out of a dark room. This is a matter of changing the direction of our love, and that change happens most deeply when we cooperate with the indwelling spirit.

The passage calls this “⟦Q 156:5.5⟧the expulsive energy of a new and sincere spiritual affection.⟦/Q⟧” The phrase holds a very deep psychological truth. The mind does not leave an empty space for long. To drive one thing out, something stronger must fill its place. “⟦Q 156:5.5⟧Beauty is always triumphant over ugliness in the hearts of all who are illuminated by the love of truth.⟦/Q⟧” As love for God and for our neighbors grows, selfish and lower desires naturally lose their footing. So spiritual growth is not a matter of lengthening the list of prohibitions, but of raising the objects of our love.

Jesus closes this teaching with the words, “⟦Q 156:5.5⟧Be not overcome by evil but rather overcome evil with good.⟦/Q⟧” This principle applies not only to inner temptations but also to our relationships with others. If we try to repay in kind those who harm us, evil grows greater; but when we answer with good, evil loses its power. The Urantia Book stresses that the religion of Jesus was not negative prohibition but the positive doing of good (159:5.10). To set our hearts not so much on what we must not do as on what we will love and do: this is the way of Jesus.

If there is a temptation or bad habit you are wrestling with today, do not merely try to hold it down by force. Instead, look for something higher and more beautiful to fill its place, and give your heart to it. When we begin to love understanding instead of anger, gratitude instead of complaint, and meaningful service instead of empty pleasure, the indwelling spirit will nurture that new affection within us. In this way we are set free not by suppression but by transformation. Temptations will still come, but their power will steadily weaken over a soul captured by a greater love.
d306.pr: Call to mind one habit you want to break, choose one better action to take its place, and practice it today.

msg: Near Caesarea-Philippi, Jesus asked his apostles who people said he was, and who they said he was. Peter confessed that he was the Deliverer, the Son of the living God, and the other apostles agreed with one accord (157:3.5). That evening after supper, Jesus, still standing, spoke to the twelve the words of today’s passage. It is an important declaration revealing upon what the brotherhood of the kingdom of heaven is built.

Jesus first says that their confession was not the result of “⟦Q 157:4.5⟧mere human knowledge.⟦/Q⟧” It was “⟦Q 157:4.5⟧a revelation of the spirit of my Father to your inmost souls.⟦/Q⟧” This point is vital. True knowledge of who Jesus is comes not only through argument or evidence, but through the insight of the Father’s spirit dwelling within us. Before it is a conclusion of the head, a confession of faith is a spiritual recognition arising in the depths of the soul. That is why, looking at the same Jesus, some see only the carpenter’s son while others see the Son of God.

Then Jesus declares that “⟦Q 157:4.5⟧upon this foundation will I build the brotherhood of the kingdom of heaven.⟦/Q⟧” In this passage the rock is not one man named Peter, but the spiritual reality gained through the insight of the Father’s spirit, the confession of living faith. “⟦Q 157:4.5⟧Upon this rock of spiritual reality will I build the living temple of spiritual fellowship.⟦/Q⟧” His temple is not a temple of stone but the living fellowship of those who have realized their sonship with God. This temple is bound to no single place or building; it is built wherever people are united in faith.

Jesus makes two promises concerning this brotherhood. One is that “⟦Q 157:4.5⟧all the forces of evil and the hosts of sin shall not prevail against this human fraternity of the divine spirit.⟦/Q⟧” The other is that the Father’s spirit “⟦Q 157:4.5⟧shall ever be the divine guide and mentor of all who enter the bonds of this spirit fellowship.⟦/Q⟧” The true guide of the spiritual brotherhood is not a man but the Father’s spirit. This is why spiritual fellowship is stronger and more lasting than any outward organization. Institutions built by men rise and fall, but a fellowship bound by the spirit endures across the ages.

At the same time, Jesus delivers to the apostles and their successors “⟦Q 157:4.5⟧the keys of the outward kingdom — the authority over things temporal.⟦/Q⟧” The care of the social and economic order needed when believers gather together was entrusted to men. Here we see an important distinction. The spiritual brotherhood is guided by the Father’s spirit; the outward organization is managed by men. When the two are confused and the outward organization is identified with spiritual authority, religion loses its original vitality (see Paper 195). Organization is necessary, but it must always be a vessel that serves spiritual fellowship.

On what rock are we standing today? If our faith leans only on loyalty to a particular organization or person, it will waver when that organization or person wavers. But if we stand on the assurance the Father’s spirit has given in the depths of the soul, the living experience of God revealed in Jesus and of our sonship, no storm can bring that foundation down. And our fellowship with those who share that experience is the very living temple Jesus built.
d307.pr: Write in one sentence what the foundation of your faith is, and see whether it is a person or a living experience.

d308.t: The Son Who Came from the Father
msg: On the afternoon of the day after Peter’s confession, Jesus for the first time spoke boldly to his apostles about his identity in a way he had never done before. The Urantia Book explains that at this time Jesus chose the third plan: to reveal his divinity and to declare directly to the twelve that he was a Son of God (157:5.2). Today’s passage is the heart of that declaration. Though he stood before them in physical presence, he said, “⟦Q 157:6.11⟧I came forth from God the Father. Before Abraham was, I am.⟦/Q⟧” It was a revelation far greater and more mysterious than the messianic expectations the apostles had cherished.

These words must have fallen on the apostles with tremendous weight. The carpenter of Nazareth with whom they had eaten, walked, and laughed was the very one who had come from the Father. Jesus says, “⟦Q 157:6.11⟧I did come forth from the Father into this world as you have known me.⟦/Q⟧” This is the astonishing truth that God is not one who hides far away, but one who has come among us in a human form we can recognize. The Urantia Book explains this as the bestowal of Michael, the Creator Son of our universe, who came to this world as the Son of Man (see Paper 120).

But Jesus at once shakes the apostles’ expectations head-on. “⟦Q 157:6.12⟧The Son of Man will not meet the expectations of your fathers as they conceived the Messiah.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 157:6.12⟧My kingdom is not of this world,⟦/Q⟧” he says. And he adds, “⟦Q 157:6.12⟧though the foxes have holes and the birds of heaven have nests, I have not where to lay my head.⟦/Q⟧” The glorious declaration that he is the Son of God and the poor reality of having nowhere even to lay his head stand side by side.

This contrast shows how the divinity of Jesus is revealed. It is not revealed in thrones, armies, and wealth, but in service, humility, and self-giving love. The apostles thought that the Son of God must surely seize power, but Jesus showed that God’s greatness lies precisely in lowliness and service. That is why he asks, “⟦Q 157:6.12⟧Can your faith comprehend the truth of these declarations?⟦/Q⟧” The way the Son of God reveals himself is not a majesty that crushes us but a love that raises us up.

The same question is put to us today. We say we believe in Jesus, yet secretly we hope he will fulfill our worldly expectations. We want a Messiah who gives success, security, and recognition. But Jesus’ kingdom is not of this world. The path of following him may at times be a path with nowhere to lay our heads. If even on that path we hold fast to the truth that he came from the Father, we gain far more than we lose. For to gain him is to gain everything.

Jesus also says that he “⟦Q 157:6.11⟧must presently leave this world and return to the work of my Father.⟦/Q⟧” He came from the Father, and he returns to the Father. We too bear a spirit that came from the Father, and we are on a journey that leads at last back to the Father. If your heart is too tightly bound to the things of this earth today, remember the Son of God who had nowhere to lay his head. Just as his true home was the Father’s embrace, our true home is there as well.
d308.pr: Find one worldly thing you secretly expect from Jesus, lay it down, and pray that you will follow him for his own sake.

msg: On Mount Hermon, Jesus was transfigured before Peter, James, and John. The three apostles saw their Master talking with two shining beings and took them to be Moses and Elijah, but The Urantia Book tells us they were in fact Gabriel and the Father Melchizedek (158:1). They had come on behalf of the Eternal Son and the Infinite Spirit to bear testimony that Jesus’ earth mission was proceeding successfully. Today’s passage is one of those that explain the meaning of the transfiguration. Overwhelmed by the sight, the three apostles fell down in fear and wonder.

Jesus welcomed this testimony. But the passage adds one important fact: “⟦Q 158:3.4⟧his Father did not indicate that the Urantia bestowal was finished.⟦/Q⟧” The glorious moment on the mountain was not the completion of his mission but a confirmation for the road that still lay ahead. Indeed, soon after coming down the mountain, Jesus began to tell his apostles of his death and resurrection (158:7). Moments of glory do not spare us the road of suffering; they give us strength to walk it. God sometimes grants us mountaintop moments too, but they are always for the everyday life we must go back down to live.

The center of the passage is the Father’s testimony. “⟦Q 158:3.4⟧Only did the unseen presence of the Father bear witness through Jesus’ Personalized Adjuster, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son; give heed to him.’⟦/Q⟧” This voice echoes the one heard at his baptism in the Jordan. The Father acknowledges the Son and, at the same time, asks one thing of men: give heed to him. This brief command is the most fundamental instruction given to all who follow Jesus.

What does it mean to give heed to him? On the mountain, Peter proposed building three tabernacles. He wanted to hold on to that moment of glory. But the Father’s voice said not to build tabernacles but to give heed to the Son. Faith is not grasping a special experience and setting up a monument to it; it is listening to the teachings of Jesus and living them out. Wondrous experiences pass, but his words lead us day by day. To give heed means more than receiving with the ear; it means answering with our lives.

We often long for special spiritual experiences. We wait for light on the mountain, a voice from heaven, a sure sign. But most days are ordinary days at the foot of the mountain. In fact, when the three apostles came down, there was an uproar below because the remaining apostles had been unable to heal the epileptic boy (158:4). The real test of the spiritual life takes place not on the mountaintop but at its foot. And what sustains us there is the one word heard on the mountain: the voice saying, “⟦Q 158:3.4⟧Give heed to him.⟦/Q⟧”

Today, be one who gives heed to Jesus. Hold one of his teachings in your heart, and let it guide your choices, words, and actions today. And ask the Thought Adjuster within you, the spirit of the Father, to help you understand that word. To give heed to the words of the Son whom the Father loves is the surest way for us to draw near to the Father’s will.
d309.pr: Choose one saying of Jesus to carry in your heart all day, and look for one chance to act on it.

d310.t: The Greatness of One Who Serves
msg: While Jesus and three of the apostles were on the mount of the transfiguration, the nine apostles left at the foot of the mountain tried and failed to heal a boy suffering from epilepsy. There was a reason for that failure. In the garden of Celsus, Jesus explained to them the cause of their defeat: though instructed to pray with their brethren on the mountain, they had fallen back into their old evil tendency of seeking special places for themselves in the kingdom of heaven (158:6.2). Today’s passage is Jesus’ penetrating diagnosis of that selfish ambition. They failed not only for lack of faith, but because their hearts were set on the wrong things.

Jesus points out that “⟦Q 158:6.3⟧no sooner does your faith grasp the identity of the Son of Man than your selfish desire for worldly preferment creeps back upon you.⟦/Q⟧” This is a very sharp observation. The moment of spiritual progress is also the moment when the temptation of pride comes calling. Not long after Peter’s great confession, the apostles began to argue among themselves about who should be greatest. The greater our spiritual insight, the greater the temptation to use it for ourselves.

Jesus declares that the kingdom “⟦Q 158:6.3⟧as you persist in conceiving it, does not exist, nor ever shall.⟦/Q⟧” And he reminds them again of the meaning of true greatness: “⟦Q 158:6.3⟧he who would be greatest in the kingdom of my Father’s spiritual brotherhood must become little in his own eyes and thus become the server of his brethren.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 158:6.3⟧Spiritual greatness consists in an understanding love that is Godlike and not in an enjoyment of the exercise of material power for the exaltation of self.⟦/Q⟧” The order of the kingdom of God turns the order of the world upside down.

The last part of the passage analyzes their failure layer by layer. “⟦Q 158:6.3⟧Your purpose was not pure. Your motive was not divine. Your ideal was not spiritual. Your ambition was not altruistic. Your procedure was not based on love, and your goal of attainment was not the will of the Father in heaven.⟦/Q⟧” This analysis is an excellent mirror in which to examine ourselves whenever we undertake anything. Even an outwardly good deed is not accompanied by spiritual power if the purpose, motive, and method within it are amiss.

This teaching applies just as fully to the communities of faith of our day. When a place of service becomes a place of influence and an office of ministry becomes a contest for status, a community loses its spiritual power. Just as the nine apostles could not heal the boy, we too, amid our strife to rise above one another, lose the power to help those who truly need help. At the Last Supper, Jesus showed the same lesson in deed when he washed the apostles’ feet (see Paper 179).

Hold up the things you do today to these questions. Is my purpose pure? Is my motive directed toward God? Is my ideal spiritual? Is my ambition altruistic? Is my method based on love? Even if you find yourself lacking before these questions, do not lose heart. The apostles were the same, yet Jesus did not give up on them. Only, today, do at least one thing not to be recognized but to serve. In heaven, one small act of service is a far greater thing than gaining a high place.
d310.pr: Choose one thing you will do today, and examine in turn whether its purpose, motive, and method are grounded in love.

d311.t: Faith Is the Sail of the Ship
msg: During the season when he taught throughout the region of the Decapolis, Jesus gave a number of instructions to the teachers and believers of the kingdom. Among them, today’s passage opens with deep compassion for the spiritual condition of men. “⟦Q 159:3.8⟧The world is filled with hungry souls who famish in the very presence of the bread of life⟦/Q⟧”; “⟦Q 159:3.8⟧men die searching for the very God who lives within them.⟦/Q⟧” These words carry the Master’s sorrow over a humanity that fails to recognize truth even when it stands so near. Even today people wander endlessly in search of meaning and peace, yet never look into the place that is nearest of all.

The tragedy is not that God is far away. On the contrary, God already dwells within each person as the Thought Adjuster. Men seek for the treasures of the kingdom “⟦Q 159:3.8⟧with yearning hearts and weary feet,⟦/Q⟧” wandering from place to place, when those treasures are “⟦Q 159:3.8⟧all within the immediate grasp of living faith.⟦/Q⟧” What they sought far away was in truth closest at hand. Our task is not to travel farther, but to recognize by faith the One who already lives within us.

Jesus likens faith to the sails of a ship. The comparison is both beautiful and exact. A sail does not add cargo to a ship; it catches the wind and gives the ship the power to move forward. In the same way, true faith does not load life with heavy duties and rules; it is “⟦Q 159:3.8⟧an addition of power, not an added burden of life.⟦/Q⟧” If we feel faith to be a burden, perhaps we have not yet raised the sail and are still straining at the oars. The wind is the spirit of God, and the sail is our faith that receives that spirit.

Jesus also says that “⟦Q 159:3.8⟧there is but one struggle for those who enter the kingdom, and that is to fight the good fight of faith.⟦/Q⟧” And he adds that “⟦Q 159:3.8⟧the believer has only one battle, and that is against doubt — unbelief.⟦/Q⟧” We often think of the religious life as an endless war against countless sins and temptations. But Jesus simplifies the matter to its heart. At the root of every struggle lies a single question: do we trust God? As trust grows, the other battles gradually lose their strength. For the one who trusts God deeply, temptation steadily loses its charm, and fear steadily loses its footing.

The battle against doubt is not the same as forbidding honest questions. The Urantia Book highly esteems the triumph of spiritual faith won by honestly overcoming intellectual doubt (155:5.10). The unbelief spoken of here is the heart that refuses to believe in God’s goodness and faithfulness, the heart that would rather trust its own fears than his love. This battle is fought anew every day. When worries flood in, when it feels as though our prayers go unanswered, we must choose trust again.

Are we, today, going hungry in the very presence of the bread of life? If you have grown weary searching for answers far away, pause for a moment and consider the spirit of the Father who lives within you. Then raise the sail of faith. When we stop rowing by our own strength and entrust our lives to the wind of the Father’s spirit, we move forward far more lightly and with far more power. Today we have only one battle to fight: the good fight of overcoming doubt and choosing trust. A ship with its sails raised crosses the sea as the wind carries it.
d311.pr: Whenever worry rises today, turn it into a prayer of trust and choose faith instead of doubt.

msg: During the Decapolis tour Jesus talked at length with Nathaniel about the Scriptures, and the Urantia Book then goes on to summarize the positive character of the Master’s religion. Jesus accepted the better parts of the Hebrew scriptures and did not hesitate to reject the inferior ones. Above all, he taught an active and aggressive righteousness that went beyond a negative or purely passive attitude (159:5.9). Today’s passage shows the heart of that teaching. The religion of Jesus was not a religion of avoiding and abstaining, but a religion of going forth and doing.

Jesus “⟦Q 159:5.10⟧did not advocate the practice of negative submission to the indignities of those who might purposely seek to impose upon the practitioners of nonresistance to evil.⟦/Q⟧” His word about turning the other cheek did not mean helplessly enduring mistreatment. It meant acting positively to lead an erring brother away from the evil path and into a better way. Jesus wanted his followers to “⟦Q 159:5.10⟧be wise and alert in the quick and positive reaction of good to evil to the end that they might effectively overcome evil with good.⟦/Q⟧”

The passage tells us, “⟦Q 159:5.10⟧Forget not, the truly good is invariably more powerful than the most malignant evil.⟦/Q⟧” This is not naive optimism but confidence in the fundamental order of the universe. Evil may seem strong for a time, but it bears within itself the seeds of its own destruction. Goodness, on the other hand, is rooted in the nature of God and so it finally prevails. With this confidence we can find the courage to do good rather than shrinking back before evil. A good deed may look small, yet it carries eternal value and never passes away in vain.

The Master taught a positive standard of righteousness: “⟦Q 159:5.10⟧Whosoever wishes to be my disciple, let him disregard himself and take up the full measure of his responsibilities daily to follow me.⟦/Q⟧” And he so lived himself in that “⟦Q 159:5.10⟧he went about doing good.⟦/Q⟧” The life of Jesus is remembered not for what he refrained from doing but for what he did. He did not stop at avoiding sin; he healed the sick, comforted the sorrowing, and went out in search of the lost. His whole life was a record of active love.

The last sentence of the passage sums it all up. He never exhorted his followers patiently to bear their obligations but rather “⟦Q 159:5.10⟧with energy and enthusiasm to live up to the full measure of their human responsibilities and divine privileges in the kingdom of God.⟦/Q⟧” If we understand the religious life only as a list of things we must not do, life shrinks and darkens. But if we understand it as good works to be done and privileges to be enjoyed, life widens and brightens. The believer’s life is not one fenced in by walls of prohibition, but one opened out into the fields of love.

Is my faith today passive or positive? If you are content simply because you did nothing wrong, think again in the light of the Master’s standard. Look back and ask whether there was some good you could have done today, someone you could have comforted, some injustice you could have set right. And tomorrow, step forward first and do at least one good thing. The path of following the One who went about doing good begins with actively practicing small kindnesses every day.
d312.pr: Choose one good thing you can do today by reaching out first to someone, and do it right away.

msg: Rodan, the Greek philosopher from Alexandria, spent many days in Galilee conversing with the disciples of Jesus. He spoke, through the eyes of Greek philosophy, about the art of living and the solving of problems, and in the course of it he described the greatest method he had learned from Jesus: “⟦Q 160:1.10⟧the isolation of worshipful meditation,⟦/Q⟧” which the Master so consistently practiced and so faithfully taught. It is deeply significant that what most impressed a philosopher about the life of Jesus was not his miracles or his sermons but this quiet habit.

Rodan says that in this habit of Jesus’ going off so frequently by himself to commune with the Father in heaven he found two things: the technique of “⟦Q 160:1.10⟧gathering strength and wisdom for the ordinary conflicts of living,⟦/Q⟧” and the technique of “⟦Q 160:1.10⟧appropriating the energy for the solution of the higher problems of a moral and spiritual nature.⟦/Q⟧” Though surrounded by crowds and busy in service, Jesus never lost his time alone with the Father. Those quiet hours were the spring that sustained all his activity. Unlike us, who cut back on prayer the busier we become, Jesus withdrew all the more deeply to the Father the busier he was.

Rodan adds that “⟦Q 160:1.10⟧even correct methods of solving problems will not compensate for inherent defects of personality or atone for the absence of the hunger and thirst for true righteousness.⟦/Q⟧” This is an important qualification. Worshipful withdrawal is not a mere technique. It bears fruit only when there is a sincere longing for God. If we merely imitate the form without the direction of the heart, the quiet time will be nothing more than rest. It is not stillness itself that renews us, but the Father whom we meet in that stillness.

In the next paragraph Rodan describes in detail what this habit of Jesus accomplished. In those seasons the Master engaged in solitary survey of the problems of living and sought “⟦Q 160:1.11⟧new stores of wisdom and energy for meeting the manifold demands of social service.⟦/Q⟧” He quickened and deepened the supreme purpose of living “⟦Q 160:1.11⟧by actually subjecting the total personality to the consciousness of contacting with divinity.⟦/Q⟧” He grasped for new and better methods of adjusting himself to the ever-changing situations of living existence, and effected those vital reconstructions and readjustments of his personal attitudes. And he did all of this “⟦Q 160:1.11⟧with an eye single to the glory of God.⟦/Q⟧”

At the center of it all was a single prayer: “⟦Q 160:1.11⟧Not my will, but yours, be done.⟦/Q⟧” Rodan speaks of breathing this prayer in sincerity. Worshipful withdrawal is not a time for pressing God to solve our problems, but a time for bringing our will into line with the Father’s will. In the paragraphs that follow, Rodan says that such worship brings the relaxation that renews the mind, the illumination that inspires the soul, and the self-understanding that erases fear (160:1.12). That time is not an escape from the world, but a return to the Father in order to go back out into the world.

How busy is our life today? Amid tasks to finish, people to meet, and problems to solve, we easily grow weary and lose our way. All the more, then, we need times of withdrawing alone as Jesus did. Even for a short while each day, lay everything down and remain in the presence of the Father. Rather than listing your problems, seek the Father’s will and readjust your attitudes. That quiet time will become a spring of strength and wisdom for going out into the world once more.
d313.pr: Spend ten minutes today alone in a quiet place, sincerely praying, “⟦Q 160:1.11⟧Not my will, but yours, be done.⟦/Q⟧”

msg: Speaking of the balance of maturity, Rodan emphasized the art of dealing with failure. Just before this, he had said that life becomes a burden of existence unless one learns how to fail gracefully, and that there is an art in defeat which noble souls always acquire (160:4.13). He also said that success may generate courage, but wisdom comes only from the experience of adjusting to the results of one’s own failures (160:4.14). Today’s passage adds the perspective of religion to this teaching.

Rodan says that it is “⟦Q 160:4.15⟧in this business of facing failure and adjusting to defeat that the far-reaching vision of religion exerts its supreme influence.⟦/Q⟧” In the moment of failure our vision often narrows. The present failure feels like everything, and it seems to decide our worth. But religion gives us the vision of eternity. We are not on this short life alone but on an endless ascent toward Paradise, and on that long journey a single failure is only one scene. Seen with the eyes of eternity, today’s failure is not an ending but part of our learning.

So Rodan says that “⟦Q 160:4.15⟧failure is simply an educational episode — a cultural experiment in the acquirement of wisdom — in the experience of the God-seeking man.⟦/Q⟧” To such men “⟦Q 160:4.15⟧defeat is but a new tool for the achievement of higher levels of universe reality.⟦/Q⟧” This does not mean that failure should be taken lightly. The pain of failure is real. It means rather that, instead of crushing us, that pain can become the material that teaches and shapes us.

The passage goes on to say something remarkable. “⟦Q 160:4.16⟧The career of a God-seeking man may prove to be a great success in the light of eternity, even though the whole temporal-life enterprise may appear as an overwhelming failure, provided each life failure yielded the culture of wisdom and spirit achievement.⟦/Q⟧” A life that failed by the world’s standards may be a successful life by heaven’s standards. Even the earthly life of Jesus seemed, in the eyes of the world, to end in the failure of the cross, yet it was no failure at all. God looks not at the splendor of results but at the soul that has grown through the process.

Finally, Rodan urges us not to make the mistake of confusing knowledge, culture, and wisdom. “⟦Q 160:4.16⟧They are related in life, but they represent vastly differing spirit values.⟦/Q⟧” Knowledge is knowing facts, and culture is the refining of life, but wisdom is the ability to embrace both facts and ideals and to guide life rightly. And wisdom is gained more deeply through failure than through success. “⟦Q 160:4.16⟧Wisdom ever dominates knowledge and always glorifies culture.⟦/Q⟧”

If your heart is heavy today because of some past failure, look at it again in the light of eternity. Consider what that failure taught you, and in what ways it made you humbler and wiser. Do not hide or deny your failure; acknowledge it honestly and draw learning up out of it. For the one who seeks God, no failure is wasted. Every fall can become, in the Father’s hands, a stepping-stone for climbing higher. The soul that does not fear failure finds the courage to try again, and that courage in the end brings forth growth.
d314.pr: Recall one past failure, write down the lesson it taught you, and give thanks for that experience.

msg: As the conversations with Rodan went on, Nathaniel and Thomas set before him the reasons why they had come to believe in the divine nature of Jesus. They offered a number of reasons, drawn from what they had seen and heard firsthand while living with the Master. Today’s passage is the eighth of these, a testimony to how naturally and intimately Jesus spoke of his relationship with God. What they put forward to persuade a philosopher was not so much logic as the experience of a life shared together.

The first thing the apostles observed was that Jesus “⟦Q 161:2.9⟧constantly talks about God as an ever-present associate in all that he does.⟦/Q⟧” For him God was not a distant abstraction but One who was with him in every moment of working, walking, and resting. “⟦Q 161:2.9⟧He goes about doing good, for God seems to be in him.⟦/Q⟧” The good deeds of Jesus were not so much the product of strenuous effort as the natural overflow of the God who was within him. The one who lives with God does not squeeze out goodness by force but lets it flow as naturally as a spring.

Second, the apostles say that “⟦Q 161:2.9⟧he makes the most astounding assertions about himself and his mission on earth, statements which would be absurd if he were not divine.⟦/Q⟧” He once declared, “⟦Q 161:2.9⟧Before Abraham was, I am.⟦/Q⟧” He dared to assert that he and the Father are one, and he said that anyone who has seen him has seen the Father. If a man of sound mind and blameless morals makes such claims, then those claims are either true or there is no way to explain them.

Yet what impressed the apostles most was not the content of these claims but the manner in which he spoke them. “⟦Q 161:2.9⟧He says and does all these tremendous things with such childlike naturalness.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 161:2.9⟧He alludes to his association with the Father in the same manner that he refers to his association with us.⟦/Q⟧” There was in him no exaggeration and no pretense. “⟦Q 161:2.9⟧He seems to be so sure about God and speaks of these relations in such a matter-of-fact way.⟦/Q⟧” This very naturalness lent his words a deep sincerity. True conviction does not raise its voice; it shows itself quietly and naturally.

This testimony shows us what a relationship with God can look like. The divinity of Jesus differs from ours, yet an intimate relationship with the Father is open to us as well. The Urantia Book teaches that through his human life Jesus showed mortals the way of living by a faith that knows God while doing the Father’s will (see Paper 196). We too can commune with the Father through the indwelling Thought Adjuster and live with God as our everyday companion.

Today, try living with God in mind not as One far away but as an ever-present associate. Remember that he is with you when you begin your work, when you meet people, and when you make decisions. Instead of grand religious language, speak to the Father naturally, as you would to a close friend. Just as Jesus lived his relationship with the Father with childlike naturalness, we too can learn day by day to walk with him in trust. As such days accumulate, we too will gradually come to resemble a life that is one with the Father.
d315.pr: Each time you begin a task or meet someone today, say silently in your heart, “Father, be with me.”

msg: On the last great day of the Feast of Tabernacles, just after the procession from the pool of Siloam had passed through the temple courts and the priests had poured the water and wine upon the altar, Jesus stood among the pilgrims and cried out that whoever thirsted should come to him and drink (162:6.1). That water-pouring ceremony symbolized the age-old hope that the spirit of God would be poured out upon the people. After the early morning service was over, Jesus went on teaching the multitude, and today’s passage is that teaching. Before the multitude of pilgrims gathered in the temple, he proclaimed the reality that lies beyond the symbol.

Jesus first reminds them of the promise of the Hebrew scriptures: “⟦Q 162:6.3⟧Behold, as the waters are poured out upon the dry ground and spread over the parched soil, so will I give the spirit of holiness to be poured out upon your children for a blessing even to your children’s children.⟦/Q⟧” And then he asks pointedly, “⟦Q 162:6.3⟧Why will you thirst for the ministry of the spirit while you seek to water your souls with the traditions of men, poured from the broken pitchers of ceremonial service?⟦/Q⟧” The image of broken pitchers is striking. However devout a ceremony may be, when it tries to take the place of reality, it becomes a broken vessel that cannot satisfy the thirst of the soul.

Yet Jesus did not condemn ceremony outright. He acknowledged that they had done well to perpetuate these symbols, even down to that day. Symbols have value in themselves. They awaken in people’s hearts a longing for God and carry hope across the generations. The problem is to keep clinging to the symbol when the reality to which it points has come. Now had come “⟦Q 162:6.3⟧the revelation of the Father of spirits through the bestowal of his Son,⟦/Q⟧” and the time was near when the spirit that the symbol pointed to would actually be poured out. A symbol is a signpost pointing the way, not the destination itself.

Jesus promises that all of this “⟦Q 162:6.3⟧will certainly be followed by the bestowal of the spirit of the Father and the Son upon the children of men.⟦/Q⟧” This promise was fulfilled at Pentecost, when the Spirit of Truth was poured out after Jesus ascended to the Father (see Paper 194). The Urantia Book teaches that this bestowal of the spirit was not limited to any particular race or class but was given to all men. Now the spirit of God is no longer confined within the ceremonies of the temple; it lives and moves in the heart of each person.

The last sentence of the passage tells us what this spirit does. “⟦Q 162:6.3⟧To every one who has faith shall this bestowal of the spirit become the true teacher of the way which leads to life everlasting.⟦/Q⟧” That way begins in “⟦Q 162:6.3⟧the kingdom of heaven on earth⟦/Q⟧” and leads on to “⟦Q 162:6.3⟧the true waters of life⟦/Q⟧” in “⟦Q 162:6.3⟧the Father’s Paradise over there.⟦/Q⟧” The Spirit of Truth teaches and guides us and makes the truth that Jesus revealed come alive within us. The one who walks with that spirit will never thirst. Wherever we are, that spirit is with us, refreshing our souls each day with new truth.

With what are we trying to satisfy the thirst of our souls today? Amid familiar rituals and habits and forms repeated over and over, we sometimes feel dry. At such times Jesus does not invite us to abandon the forms, but to go on to the living reality to which they point. When you pray and worship today, open your heart with an awareness of the Father and the Spirit of Truth who stand beyond the act itself. Then the water of life will begin to spring up within you.
d316.pr: Choose one act of faith you have done out of habit, reflect on its meaning, and do it again today with a living heart.

msg: During the Feast of Tabernacles Jesus discoursed in the temple on spiritual freedom. At this time the religious leaders in Jerusalem were watching for an opportunity to arrest him, yet Jesus taught openly and without fear. In today’s passage he reveals the mark of the true disciple and the source of true freedom: “⟦Q 162:7.2⟧If my words abide in you and you are minded to do the will of my Father, then are you truly my disciples. You shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.⟦/Q⟧”

The conditions of discipleship Jesus names are two. One is that his words abide in us; the other is that we be minded to do the will of the Father. It is not enough to hear his words once and admire them. Those words must remain within us and shape our thoughts and attitudes. And at the center must be the will to do the Father’s will. Truth sets us free not when we assent to it with the mind, but only when we have a heart that intends to live it. For the words of Jesus to abide in us means that they become the standard of our judgments and choices.
