His hearers objected: “⟦Q 162:7.2⟧We are the children of Abraham, and we are in bondage to none; how then shall we be made free?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus makes clear that he does not speak of “⟦Q 162:7.2⟧outward subjection to another’s rule⟦/Q⟧”; he refers to “⟦Q 162:7.2⟧the liberties of the soul.⟦/Q⟧” And he says, “⟦Q 162:7.2⟧Everyone who commits sin is the bond servant of sin.⟦/Q⟧” A person may be politically free, may be of noble lineage, and yet within be the slave of habits, desires, and fears. The deepest bondage lies not without but within.

Jesus then gives the illustration of the servant and the son. “⟦Q 162:7.2⟧The bond servant is not likely to abide forever in the master’s house,⟦/Q⟧” but “⟦Q 162:7.2⟧the son does remain in his father’s house.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 162:7.2⟧If, therefore, the Son shall make you free, shall make you sons, you shall be free indeed.⟦/Q⟧” True freedom comes from sonship. The servant works out of fear and duty, but the son abides in his father’s house in love and trust. To realize that we are sons of God is the key to release from every bondage. The son does not fear being driven out of his father’s house.

The gospel of Jesus was above all a gospel of spiritual liberation. He came to set men free from the burden of legalism, from the religion of fear, and from the habits of sin. His teaching to go beyond the religion of authority to the religion of the spirit was an invitation to that same freedom (see Paper 155). But this freedom is not license. The freedom of a son of God is not the freedom to do whatever one pleases, but the freedom to choose the Father’s will with joy. When one who was a slave of sin becomes a son of love, he is at last truly free.

What is it that binds you today? If there is a habit you cannot break, a fear you cannot shake off, or a resentment you cannot let go, then rather than trying to cut it off by willpower alone, first take deeply to heart the truth that you are a son of the Father. And meditate every day so that the words of Jesus abide in you. Truth does not let us stop at knowing; it makes us live. That truth will set our souls free today. And a soul that has been set free gladly spends that freedom in serving others.
d317.pr: Write down one habit or fear that binds you, and beside it write, “I am a child of the Father.”

d318.t: The One Thing to Let Go
msg: Matadormus, a wealthy young man, came to Jesus in earnest. He had lived by the law and sincerely desired to become one of the seventy. But when the Master told him to part with his wealth, his face fell, and he went away sorrowful. Commenting on this scene, today’s passage says that “⟦Q 163:2.7⟧almost every human being has some one thing which is held on to as a pet evil, and which the entrance into the kingdom of heaven requires as a part of the price of admission.⟦/Q⟧” This brief scene reveals how personal and precise the door of the kingdom of heaven is. The Master does not require the same thing of everyone; he sees straight through to what binds each soul most deeply.

What deserves our attention here is that Jesus did not condemn wealth as evil in itself. Another passage in the same paper makes plain that Jesus never taught that it was wrong to possess wealth. The problem was not the wealth but the place it held in the heart of Matadormus. For him, his possessions were the security he leaned on before God, the pillar of his very identity. Because the Master loved the man, he put his finger precisely on the cord that held his soul fast. The Master’s demand was not meant to make him poor but to make him free.

The passage adds a surprising fact. “⟦Q 163:2.7⟧If Matadormus had parted with his wealth, it probably would have been put right back into his hands for administration as treasurer of the seventy.⟦/Q⟧” God is not One who seeks to take things away from us. What he wants is for us to let go of the way we clutch them, our attachment. What we offer with open hands is often entrusted back to us for a higher purpose. Letting go is not a loss but a reappointment as a steward. So the heart of letting go lies less in what we give up than in making clear who is the master of our lives. Whether wealth or talents or relationships, they find their proper place only when they become instruments in the service of the Father’s will.

Matadormus later obeyed the Master’s injunction and became the treasurer of the Jerusalem church, but by then it was too late to work at the Master’s side as one of the seventy. Postponing obedience has its cost as well. The hour of spiritual decision does not wait, and a call left unanswered now, even if it comes again in another form, is not quite the same as the first opportunity. God always receives even late obedience, but the joy and companionship that early obedience could have known remain missed. The habit of responding at once when the heart is moved is one of the surest paths of spiritual growth.

Each of us, too, has that one thing. For one it is money; for another, honor or the craving for recognition; for still another, an old resentment or a secretly cherished habit. Because it is usually the part we least want touched, we seldom recognize it ourselves. Today, rest quietly before the Thought Adjuster and ask honestly what it is that you hold on to more tightly than God. Then place it in the Father’s hands. If it is his will, you will receive it back in a healthier form.
d318.pr: Write down the one thing you cling to more tightly than God, and offer a prayer entrusting it to the Father.
